title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
hook: a song that is nothing but a string of names, and the Gita verse where the word for singing God's glory turns up

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan repertoire: Rama's name, a lamp set on the doorstep of the tongue. Before a hard conversation, what did you set there? Day nine hundred ninety.

Govinda jaya jaya, Gopala jaya jaya. Radha Ramana Hari, Govinda jaya jaya. Read it on paper and it barely looks like a song. No story, no request, no rhyme to speak of. Just names, and the word jaya, victory, hung between them like lanterns on a wire. A kirtan can ride that line up to a fast, clapping peak and then let it fall back to a whisper. Someone hearing it for the first time might ask where the meaning is. The answer is in the names themselves, and in one verse of the Bhagavad Gita.
screen: `GOVINDA JAYA JAYA.` → `NAMES LIKE LANTERNS ON A WIRE.` → `WHERE IS THE MEANING?`

segments.voice: Each name in the song is a small portrait of Krishna. Govinda and Gopala both belong to the cowherd years in Vraja, the boy among the cows and the herders. Hari is a name of Vishnu, and devotees honor Krishna as one with Vishnu. Radha Ramana is the one who delights Radha, so the song quietly brings her into the room too. String the names together and you've told a story without telling it. Anyone who knows the stories hears them pass by. Now the Gita. In chapter nine, Krishna describes the great-souled ones who turn to him. In paraphrase: always singing my glory, striving, firm in their vows, bowing to me with devotion, they worship me, ever joined. The word there for singing his glory is kirtayantah, and you can hear kirtan in it. So the practice the room is doing has a place in the Gita itself. And it isn't presented as an extra for musical people. It's set alongside striving and keeping vows, as part of how the great-souled live. The Bhagavata Purana adds a voice from inside the practice. The sage Narada, who wanders the worlds with his vina, says that when he sings of the Lord's deeds, the Lord appears quickly in his heart, as if called. That's the hope a kirtan carries, quietly, every time a name goes out and comes back. Not that a song explains God. That a name, sung with attention, can work like a call. Which is why, for devotees, the song doesn't need more words. The names are already doing the calling.
screen: `EACH NAME, A SMALL PORTRAIT.` · `THE GITA: ALWAYS SINGING MY GLORY.` · `NARADA SINGS, AND THE LORD APPEARS.` · `A NAME SUNG WITH ATTENTION CALLS.` · then, large: `THE NAMES DO THE CALLING.`

segments.voice: Settle where you are. Bring to mind a few names you've called out in your life. A parent, a friend, a child, a pet at the door. Notice how each name carries a whole person with it, and how your voice changes for each one. Let them go. If you pray, you can take one name of God from your own tradition and say it silently, slowly, the way you'd call someone you hoped would come. If not, rest with the feeling of calling and being called. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: Govinda jaya jaya, a string of Krishna's names, each one a small portrait, sung like a call.
Your line: kirtan repertoire, twenty songs. Today, when you say someone's name, say it once with full attention, as if you were calling them, and notice their face. Day nine hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Krishna devotees sing Govinda jaya jaya and similar strings of names at kirtans and in homes, often speeding up toward a clapping peak and slowing again to a hush.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: kirtayantah, singing the glory, the Gita's word in chapter nine; you can hear kirtan in it.

notes: Index title/word/carry kept exactly; spoken carry reads '(20 songs)' as 'twenty songs'.
Gita 9.14 (satatam kirtayanto mam yatantas ca drdha-vratah, namasyantas ca mam bhaktya nitya-yukta upasate) paraphrased; confirm.
Bhagavata 1.6.33 (Narada: as I sing of his deeds, he quickly appears in my heart as if called); confirm verse number and paraphrase.
'kirtayantah, from the same family as kirtan': both from the root kirt-, to mention, praise. This is a word-family statement; confirm it is acceptable under the etymology rule.
Glosses of Govinda/Gopala (cowherd years), Hari (name of Vishnu) and Radha Ramana (the one who delights Radha) are kept as glosses, not etymologies; confirm wording.
The chant 'Govinda jaya jaya, Gopala jaya jaya, Radha Ramana Hari, Govinda jaya jaya' is traditional; no author given. Confirm the commonly sung wording.
Day 986 covered the Bhagavata's tenth book; this day only names the cowherd years in passing to avoid repeating it.

Editor pass: dropped 'old' from Hari and reframed 'Krishna as Vishnu come to earth' as 'devotees honor Krishna as one with Vishnu' (fair to traditions that see Krishna as the source); replaced the word-family claim (kirtayantah 'from the same family as kirtan') with 'you can hear kirtan in it'; the closing claim is now attributed to devotees rather than stated by the narrator; practice opener varied.
Audit: read in full; no change. Gita 9.14 (kirtayantah) and Bhagavata 1.6.33 (Narada, vina, appears as if called) check out.
